newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Masood hits Afghan Taleban on second front.
newsitem.headline: Masood hits Afghan Taleban on second front.

text.p: Afghanistan's former military chief, Ahmad Shah Masood, hit back on Tuesday at the Taleban militia that drove him out of Kabul and back into his Panjsher valley base by launching an attack in the narrow Salang Pass, Taleban fighters said.

They said Basir Solangi, Masood's commander in the Salang Pass who withdrew north into territory controlled by Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum as the Taleban advanced from Kabul, attacked through the pass and over the steep mountainsides around breakfast time.
The Taleban fighters said Dostum's men were not involved in the fighting, in which the two sides exchanged artillery, mortar and small arms fire throughout the day.

Dostum, meanwhile, met Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani on a highway east of Mazar-i-Sharif on Tuesday to explore forming a common front against Taleban forces, and Dostum told reporters that Masood was also expected in Mazar-i-Sharif by Wednesday.
It was the first meeting between Rabbani and Dostum in three years. Rivalry between Dostum and Masood led Dostum to split from the government in 1994.

Western reporters said they saw two unidentified warplanes bomb Taleban positions in the winding pass through the Hindu Kush. Masood flew several Soviet-era MiG-21s out of Kabul as the Taleban approached the city, and Dostum has a small air force.
Tuesday's fighting appeared certain to heighten tensions between Dostum and the Taleban, who have taken three-quarters of Afghanistan in their two years of existence.
"Dostum gave the order for the attack," said one Taleban fighter manning a road block in the Salang Pass.
There was no word on the outcome of the fighting, but the Taleban fighters said their front line, previously some five km (three miles) south of Dostum's, had moved forward.
Dostum moved armour and men south of the Salang Tunnel, a key choke point on the road from Kabul through the Hindu Kush to his base at Mazar-i-Sharif, as the Taleban took the Afghan capital.

Tuesday's attack drew armaments and men from the Taleban effort to force their way in to the Panjsher valley through a narrow gorge. Several tanks, truck-mounted multiple rocket launchers, anti-aircraft guns and men headed north along the Salang from the entrance to the Panjsher.

There, the Taleban kept up a steady stream of artillery and mortar fire on a craggy hilltop parallel to two guarding the entrance to the gorge, which they have already taken in a campaign that began on Saturday.

There was occasional answering fire from Masood's men, but Taleban fighters at the gorge said their forces had not moved forward on Tuesday and did not know when they would be ordered onto the offensive.

Acting Foreign Minister Mullah Mohammed Ghous said on Monday he feared that if Dostum and Masood did team up they would prolong Afghanistan's 17-year war, which he said the Taleban were dedicated to ending.
The new government, which Ghous described as a caretaker administration, has said it wants to negotiate with Dostum, not fight him, but Ghous suggested it would if Dostum began hostilities.
A new alliance between Masood and Dostum would be a major problem for the purist Islamic Taleban leadership, which has imposed the Islamic Sharia law wherever it has taken control.
They have swept all before them since the movement was born in religious schools in refugee camps in Pakistan.

But in four days of fighting in the Panjsher gorge, they have penetrated a mere 500 yards (metres) into the territory of the famed general who repulsed repeated attempts to capture it in the 1980s by Soviet troops backing a then-communist govennment in Kabul.
Dostum favours a liberal interpretation of Islam. His men often drink, an abhorrence to the Taleban, and are among the toughest fighters in a land of tough fighters.
